narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 51% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped just over 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking in the third year of law school was the strongest influence, and it pushed the prediction toward failure. You placed in the bottom decile (1 out of 10) among your classmates, well below the average of roughly the middle of the class for students who were accepted. This low ranking signaled to the model a higher risk that you would struggle with the bar exam.

Your undergraduate GPA worked in the opposite direction. At 3.70 it is noticeably stronger than the 3.23 average of accepted students, so this feature pulled the prediction toward passing and helped offset some of the concern.

Your LSAT score of 34 also pulled the prediction downward toward success, but its effect was smaller than the impact of your third-year ranking. Even though the score is only a few points below the accepted average of 37, the model still saw your overall profile as slightly more likely to result in failure than success.

Because the dominant factor was your third-year performance, the clearest next step is to strengthen that area if you retake courses or seek additional support before reapplying. Improving your upper-level grades would directly address the element that weighed most heavily against you.
